According to arXiv 2603.26983, a technical challenge that arises when applying Art. 50 II watermarking to synthetic data used for AI training is the fundamental tension between human-readable labeling and machine-readability. Watermarks designed to be discernible to humans can impede the training of AI models, as they may evolve into features that the AI systems learn to recognize, jeopardizing the integrity of the training data. This creates a conflict between the regulatory requirement for persistent labeling and the technical need for clean, unadulterated data in model training pipelines.

In comparison, fact-checking systems face challenges related to the interleaving of human and AI contributions, which complicates the marking process. When journalists review and edit AI-generated outputs, the boundary between AI-generated and human-authored content becomes blurred, making it impossible to maintain a clear provenance chain. Unlike the synthetic data case, where a dual-version API can separate watermarked and watermark-free outputs, no equivalent solution exists for fact-checking pipelines, as the human editorial process destroys the marking signals required for machine-readable compliance. 

Thus, while both cases highlight the difficulties of maintaining effective marking under regulatory requirements, the specific challenges differ: synthetic data struggles with the integrity of training data due to watermarking, whereas fact-checking systems struggle with the loss of provenance due to human intervention.
